slides.headline: Up to 97% of its chases end in a catch.
slides.sub: Meet the dragonfly, one of the most effective aerial predators

slides.label: of chases won by Blue Dashers hunting fruit flies
slides.body: Filmed in greenhouse trials. Three other skimmer and meadowhawk species caught fruit flies in 89–93% of chases.
slides.source: Combes et al., Integr. Comp. Biol. (2013)

slides.headline: The twist: bigger prey escapes more
slides.body: In the same trials, success fell to 67–79% on mosquitoes, 56–67% on houseflies and 20–43% on deerflies.
slides.source: Combes et al., Integr. Comp. Biol. (2013)

slides.headline: It flies to where the prey is going
slides.body: Its head locks onto the target while the body steers onto the prey's flight path, guided by predictions, much like your brain plans a reach.

slides.headline: Eyes that wrap almost all the way round
slides.body: Huge compound eyes cover most of the head, giving a field of vision approaching 360°. Some species have sharper zones for spotting flying insects.

slides.headline: Send this to someone who swats mosquitoes all summer.
slides.body: Real numbers, real studies, no hype. Follow @earthspirit_nature.
sources: Combes et al. (2013) Integrative & Comparative Biology 53(5):787–798

caption:
Dragonflies (Anisoptera) catch prey in up to 97% of chases. The Blue Dasher (Pachydiplax longipennis) set that mark.

There are roughly 3,000 dragonfly species, and Britannica notes they sometimes take prey weighing 60% as much as they do. The 97% figure comes from greenhouse trials with fruit flies; against bigger, faster deerflies, success dropped as low as 20%.

Swipe for how they do it. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Combes et al. 2013, Integrative & Comparative Biology; Mischiati et al. 2015, Nature.

Save this for the next time a dragonfly zips past at the pond.
